grammar.title: Ἵστημι· ἔστησα καὶ ἔστην
grammar.rule: ἔστησε — τί; (τὸν θώρακα, τὸ στράτευμα) · ἔστη, ἐπέστη, εἱστήκει — αὐτός · ἵστημι στήσω ἔστησα ↔ ἵσταμαι ἔστην ἕστηκα

tables.caption: ἵστημι in the story: who stands? Transitive forms answer τί; (what was set up?); intransitive forms have no object

grammar.note_en:
ἵστημι is the verb of standing, and it does two jobs. Some of its forms are transitive: someone makes something else stand, sets it up or brings it to a halt, and the verb has an object. Others are intransitive: the subject itself stands, stands up or stops, and there is no object. Ask the question the rule asks, τί; ‘what was set up?’ If the sentence answers it with an accusative, the form is transitive.

The two aorists divide the work. The first aorist ἔστησα, ἔστησας, ἔστησε(ν), which adds σ to the stem στη- like any sigmatic aorist, is transitive: Gryllus τὸν παλαιὸν θώρακα πρὸ τῆς θύρας ἔστησεν, ‘set the old breastplate up in front of the door’ (s001), and Clearchus τὸ στράτευμα ἔστησεν ὥσπερ εἰς ἐξέτασιν, ‘drew the army up as if for a review’ (s059). The future στήσω ‘I shall set up’ goes with it. The second (root) aorist ἔστην, ἔστης, ἔστη, with long η in every person and no added σ, is intransitive: ‘I stood (up), I stopped’. Philesia ἀνέστη, ‘stood up’ (s101); Thymos αὐτῷ παρέστη, ‘came and stood beside him’ (s112).

The perfect ἕστηκα is intransitive too, and it has present meaning: ‘I have taken my stand’, so ‘I stand, I am standing’ (you know τέθνηκε ‘is dead’ the same way). Its pluperfect, with the augment ει-, means ‘was standing’: Sosias remembers ἐν τῷ ἡλίῳ πολὺν χρόνον εἱστήκεμεν, ‘we stood a long time in the sun’ (s060), and Gryllus looks at the door ὅπου ὁ θώραξ εἱστήκει, ‘where the breastplate was standing’ (s042). The present splits by voice: active ἵστημι ‘I set up’, middle ἵσταμαι ‘I stand, I take my stand’ (ὁ Σωσίας τίνι παρίσταται; ‘whom does Sosias stand beside?’, s115).

So the chapter’s two pictures belong together. Gryllus ἔστησε the breastplate: he did the setting up, and the breastplate is his object. Afterwards it εἱστήκει, it stood there by itself. In the same way Clearchus set the army up (ἔστησεν) and the soldiers stood (εἱστήκεμεν).

Compounds keep the split. ὁ Κλέαρχος τὸ στράτευμα ἐπέστησεν, ‘halted the army’ (s016), is transitive; in the next sentence τὸ στράτευμα ἐπέστη, ‘the army halted’ (s017), is intransitive.

One form belongs to both aorists: ἔστησαν is the third person plural of ἔστησα (‘they set up’) and of ἔστην (‘they stood’). The chapter avoids it; when you meet it, look for an object.

For the active aorists and future contrasted here, look for two things: an added σ after the stem στη- (ἔστη-σα, στή-σω: ‘set up, make stand’) or no added σ (ἔστη-ν: ‘stood’), and an accusative that answers τί;. The perfect ἕστηκα and its pluperfect are always ‘stand, was standing’, and in the present the middle ἵσταμαι is the one that means ‘stand’.

parergon.title: οὐ τῶν νικώντων ἐστί: the genitive ‘it is the part of’
parergon.body_en: A genitive after εἶναι can say whose business, right or mark something is. Clearchus answered Phalinus ὅτι οὐ τῶν νικώντων εἴη τὰ ὅπλα παραδιδόναι, ‘that it was not for victors to hand over their arms’ (s043), and Gryllus throws the same line at Sosias: οὐ τῶν νικώντων ἐστὶ τὰ ὅπλα παραδιδόναι (s054). In Xenophon’s own words Clearchus says τῶν γὰρ μάχην νικώντων καὶ τὸ ἄρχειν ἐστί, ‘for ruling, too, belongs to those who win the battle’ (s023). The infinitive is the subject; the genitive is the predicate: ‘is of the victors’.

families.spelling_note: Both are ἵστημι with a preverb, and both keep its two halves: first aorist ἐπ-έ-στησεν ‘halted (the army)’ (s016) against root aorist ἐπ-έ-στη ‘halted’ (s017). Before the rough breathing of ἵστημι, ἐπι- becomes ἐφ-: ἐφ-ίστημι; with the augment (ἔστησα has a smooth breathing) the π returns: ἐπ-έ-στησεν. παρα- loses its α before a vowel: παρ-ίσταται, παρ-έ-στη. ἐφίστημι is not simply ‘stand upon’: with an army it means ‘halt’, and with a place ‘post (soldiers) over it’ (στρατιώτας ἐπὶ τῇ σκηνῇ ἐπέστησεν, s085). παρίστημι is ‘stand beside’, and in the quarrel standing beside someone is taking his or her side: ὁ Διόδωρος τῇ μητρὶ παρέστη (s113); ὁ δὲ Σωσίας τίνι παρίσταται; (s115).
